text: Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan (5 September 1888 – 17 April 1975) was an Indian academic, philosopher, and statesman who served as Vice President of India from 1952 to 1962 and President of India from 1962 to 1967. He was ambassador of India to the Soviet Union from 1949 to 1952 and held key academic positions, including vice-chancellor of Andhra University from 1931 to 1936 and vice-chancellor of Banaras Hindu University from 1939 to 1948. Radhakrishnan was awarded a knighthood in 1931, the Bharat Ratna in 1954, and honorary membership of the British Royal Order of Merit in 1963. He was also a founder of HelpAge India. Born as Sarvepalli Radhakrishnayya in a Telugu-speaking Niyogi Brahmin family in Tiruttani, now in Tiruvallur district of Tamil Nadu, he was the fourth of six siblings. His father was a subordinate revenue official in the service of a local Zamindar. He received his primary education at K. V. High School in Thiruttani and later attended Hermansburg Evangelical Lutheran Mission School in Tirupati and Government High Secondary School, Walajapet. Radhakrishnan studied philosophy by chance after receiving textbooks from a cousin who had graduated from Madras Christian College, where he began his education at age 16. He graduated in 1907 and completed his master's degree there. His bachelor's thesis, "The Ethics of the Vedanta and its Metaphysical Presuppositions," published when he was twenty, responded to criticism that Vedanta lacked ethics. The critique of Christian teachers like William Meston and Alfred George Hogg disturbed him and motivated his lifelong study of Indian philosophy and defense of Hinduism against "uninformed Western criticism." He commended Hogg as "my distinguished teacher" and "one of the greatest Christian thinkers we had in India." Radhakrishnan expressed his anguish against British critics in *The Ethics of the Vedanta*, quoting Max Müller to argue that Vedanta includes ethics throughout its structure and that its philosophers are immune to worldly temptations. He introduced "The Spirit of Abheda," emphasizing that individuals should regard all others as co-equals and treat them as ends, not means, and that the Vedanta demands respect for human dignity. He married Sivakamu in May 1903 at age 14, when she was 10; they had five daughters and one son, Sarvepalli Gopal, who became a historian. Many of his family members pursued careers in academia, public policy, medicine, law, banking, business, publishing, and other fields. Former cricketer VVS Laxman is his great-grandnephew. They were married for 52 years, with Sivakamu dying on 26 November 1956. In 1909, he joined the Department of Philosophy at Madras Presidency College, and in 1918 became Professor of Philosophy at the University of Mysore, where he taught at Maharaja's College. He authored *The Philosophy of Rabindranath Tagore* (1918) and *The Reign of Religion in Contemporary Philosophy* (1920). In 1921, he took up the King George V Chair of Mental and Moral Science at the University of Calcutta and delivered the Hibbert Lecture at Oxford in 1929, published as *An Idealist View of Life*. In 1929, he was appointed to Manchester College, Oxford, where he lectured on Comparative Religion. He was knighted in June 1931 and formally invested in March 1932, though he ceased using the title after Indian independence, preferring the academic title "Doctor." In 1936, he was named Spalding Professor of Eastern Religion and Ethics at Oxford and elected a Fellow of All Souls College. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1936 and 1937, with further nominations continuing into the 1960s. In 1939, he was invited to become Vice-Chancellor of Banaras Hindu University, a position he held until 1948. Radhakrishnan began his political career late in life, motivated by his pride in Hindu culture and defense of Hinduism against Western criticism. He represented India at UNESCO (1946–1952) and was elected to the Constituent Assembly. He was a sponsor of the Peoples' World Convention (PWC) in 1950–51 in Geneva, Switzerland, alongside Albert Einstein. Radhakrishnan was a prominent spokesman of Neo-Vedanta, grounding his philosophy in Advaita Vedanta but reinterpreting it for contemporary understanding. He acknowledged the reality and diversity of the world of experience as grounded in Brahman and reinterpreted Shankara's maya as a "subjective misperception of the world as ultimately real." Intuition, or religious experience, is central to his philosophy as a self-certifying, self-evidencing, and self-luminous source of knowledge. He was influenced by William James, F. H. Bradley, Henri Bergson, Friedrich von Hügel, and Swami Vivekananda. Radhakrishnan discerned eight sorts of experience and viewed theology and creeds as intellectual formulations of religious intuitions. He ranked religions hierarchically based on their apprehension of religious experience, placing Advaita Vedanta at the highest level. He saw Hinduism as a scientific religion based on facts apprehended through intuition or religious experience, arguing that philosophy of religion must become empirical and grounded in religious experience. He stated that the truths of the ṛṣis are not derived from logical reasoning but from spiritual intuition, dṛṣti or vision, and that the Vedas represent the authority of facts. In *The Hindu View of Life*, he described a hierarchy of religious practices, with worshippers of the absolute at the highest rank, followed by those of the personal God, incarnations of Rama and Krishna, deities, ancestors, sages, and finally worshippers of petty forces and spirits.

The seers who could perceive eternal truths by elevating their life-spirit to the universal spirit are considered pioneer researchers in the spiritual realm, seeing beyond what their followers perceive. Their teachings stem not from fleeting visions but from continuous, lived experiences of spiritual presence and power. When the Vedas are regarded as the highest authority, it means that the most rigorous authority is that of factual experience. From his writings compiled in *The Hindu View of Life*, Upton Lectures, Delivered at Manchester College, Oxford, 1926, Radhakrishnan stated that Hinduism emphasizes steady progress in understanding God, with worshippers of the absolute at the highest level, followed by those of the personal God, then those of Rama, Krishna, and Buddha; below them are worshippers of deities, ancestors, and sages, and lowest are those who worship petty forces and spirits. The deities of some are in water, those of the advanced in the heavens, those of children in wooden or stone images, but the sage finds God in his deeper self; the man of action in fire, the man of feeling in the heart, and the weak in idols, while the strong in spirit find God everywhere. The seers see the supreme in the self, not in images. Radhakrishnan viewed Advaita Vedanta as the best representation of Hinduism because it is rooted in intuition, contrasting with the "intellectually mediated interpretations" of other religions. He rejected accusations of "quietism" and "world denial," instead emphasizing the ethic of social service and offering a modern interpretation of classical terms like tat-tvam-asi. According to Radhakrishnan, Vedanta is not a religion but religion itself in its most universal and deepest sense. He believed that all other religions, including what he considered lower forms of Hinduism, are interpretations of Advaita Vedanta, thus Hinduising all religious traditions. Despite his familiarity with Western culture and philosophy, Radhakrishnan criticized Western philosophers for being influenced by their own cultural theological biases. He was one of the world's most prominent and influential twentieth-century scholars of comparative religion and philosophy. His defense of Hindu traditions has been highly influential both in India and the West; in India, his ideas contributed to the formation of the nation-state, and his writings helped establish Vedanta as "the essential worldview of Hinduism." In the West, his interpretations and emphasis on spiritual experience made Hinduism more accessible and contributed to its influence on modern spirituality. Figures like Vivekananda and Radhakrishnan exemplify Vedanta's journey to the West, where it nourished the spiritual needs of Europeans and Americans in the early twentieth century. Radhakrishnan was highly regarded; Paul Artur Schillp called him an exemplary living "bridge" between East and West, deeply rooted in Indian traditions and equally at home in Western philosophy. Hawley noted that Radhakrishnan’s focus on experience and his deep knowledge of Western philosophical and literary traditions earned him a reputation as a bridge-builder between India and the West, and he is often seen as a representative of Hinduism to the West. His long writing career and numerous publications have shaped Western understanding of Hinduism, India, and the East. However, his ideas have faced criticism for their perennialist and universalist claims and the use of an east–west dichotomy. Radhakrishnan asserted an underlying "divine unity" from the Upanishadic seers to modern figures like Tagore and Gandhi, and an essential commonality between philosophical and religious traditions across diverse cultures—a theme shared by Rene Guenon, the Theosophical Society, and the modern popularity of Eastern religions. Since the 1970s, perennialism has been criticized for essentialism, with social-constructionists arguing that religious experiences are shaped by cultural learning rather than innate feelings like a sensus numinosus. Rinehart noted that modern Hindu thought is a historical product, developed over the past two centuries, and that Radhakrishnan, educated by missionaries and influenced by Western views, used that understanding to counter Western critiques. The elevation of Vedanta as the essence of Hinduism and Advaita Vedanta as the "paradigmatic example of the mystical nature of the Hindu religion" by colonial Indologists and neo-Vedantins served Hindu nationalists, who used it to unite Hindus against colonialism. This has been criticized by Sucheta Mazumdar and Vasant Kaiwar, who argue that Indian nationalist leaders operated within a politicized religious framework and made extravagant claims about Oriental civilization, with Radhakrishnan’s statement that "the Vedanta is not a religion but religion itself" being typical. Rinehart also criticized the inclusivity of Radhakrishnan’s approach, which subsumes religious differences under Vedantic truth, leading to communalism—the idea that people of one religion share common economic, social, and political interests opposed to those of others. Rinehart notes that Hindu religiosity plays a key role in the nationalist movement and that the neo-Hindu discourse emerged from the ideas of Rammohan Roy and Vivekananda, though he acknowledges no direct causal link to militant Hindu agendas. Colonialism left lasting impacts on how Indians understand themselves, and these influences are evident in Radhakrishnan’s work. Hawley points out that Radhakrishnan’s division between East and West—East as spiritual and mystical, West as rational and logical—was constructed during the 18th and 19th centuries and is "imagined," reflecting neither the realities of East nor West. Since the 1990s, debates have emerged among scholars about colonial influences on the construction and representation of Hinduism, with Western Indologists seeking more neutral, informed portrayals and Indian scholars aiming for knowledge grounded in Indian traditions. Radhakrishnan’s appointment as a southerner to the most important philosophy chair in India in the north was resented by the Bengali intellectual elite, and The Modern Review became a key outlet for criticism. Soon after arriving in Calcutta in 1921, his writings were regularly criticized. When he published *Indian Philosophy* in two volumes (1923 and 1927), The Modern Review questioned his use of sources, particularly the lack of references to Bengali scholars. However, in an editor’s note, the journal acknowledged it could not review the book. In the January 1929 issue, Jadunath Sinha claimed parts of his 1922 doctoral thesis, *Indian Psychology of Perception*, published in 1925, were copied by Radhakrishnan into the chapter on the Yoga system of Patanjali in *Indian Philosophy II* (1927). Sinha and Radhakrishnan exchanged letters in The Modern Review, presenting 110 instances of "borrowings." Radhakrishnan responded, stating both had used the same classical texts, that his translations were standard, and that similarities were unavoidable; he also claimed he had been lecturing on the subject before publishing and that his book was ready by 1924, before Sinha’s thesis. Scholars like Kuppuswami Sastri, Ganganath Jha, and Nalini Ganguli confirmed Radhakrishnan had distributed the notes since 1922. Ramananda Chatterjee, editor of The Modern Review, refused to publish a letter by Nalini Ganguli confirming this, continuing to publish Sinha’s letters. Professor Muirhead, general editor of Radhakrishnan’s publisher, confirmed the publication was delayed for three years due to Radhakrishnan’s stay in the United States. In summer 1929, the dispute escalated into a legal battle; Radhakrishnan filed a defamation suit against Sinha and Chatterjee, demanding Rs. 100,000, and Sinha filed a copyright infringement suit against Radhakrishnan, demanding Rs. 20,000. The suits were settled in May 1933, with the terms not disclosed, and all allegations in the pleadings and in the journal were withdrawn. Commemorative stamps released by India Post include one for Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan in 1988. A documentary film about Radhakrishnan, titled *Sarvepalli Radhakrishna*, was directed by N. S. Thapa and produced by the Government of India's Films Division. Several books have been published on Radhakrishnan.
